name: Ganirelix
evidenceNote: FDA-approved since 1999 on the strength of controlled IVF trials, and supported by a Cochrane review of 73 randomized trials comparing GnRH antagonists with the older agonist protocols.
summary: Ganirelix is a daily IVF injection that blocks the brain's ovulation signal so eggs are not released early. FDA-approved since 1999.
keyTakeaway: Ganirelix is a synthetic ten-amino-acid peptide that blocks the receptor for gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) in the pituitary. During IVF it is injected under the skin once a day to stop a premature surge of luteinizing hormone, which could release eggs before retrieval. The FDA approved it in 1999. In a North American phase 3 trial, ongoing pregnancy rates were 30.8% with ganirelix and 36.4% with a long leuprolide protocol, with fewer injection days. Across many trials, antagonists like ganirelix lower the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. It must not be used during pregnancy.

blocks.text: Ganirelix acetate is a synthetic decapeptide, a chain of ten amino acids, built from the natural hormone GnRH with six of its positions swapped for altered amino acids [1]. Those changes turn a hormone that switches the pituitary on into a molecule that blocks it. It comes as a ready-to-use solution in prefilled syringes for injection under the skin [1].

It is used only in fertility medicine. Organon holds the original approval [4], and generic versions exist, including one sold by Sun Pharma under the brand name Fyremadel [5]. Treatment lasts days, not months: it runs for part of a single ovarian stimulation cycle and then stops.

The hypothalamus releases GnRH in pulses, and each pulse tells the pituitary to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Midway through a natural cycle, a large LH surge triggers ovulation. In IVF, doctors stimulate the ovaries to grow several follicles at once and then collect the eggs at a planned time. If the body launches its own LH surge first, the eggs can be released and lost before retrieval [1].

Ganirelix sits on the GnRH receptor and keeps the natural hormone from binding. LH falls more than FSH, and because it is a blocker rather than a stimulator, there is no initial burst of hormones before suppression begins [1]. Its effect is fast and reversible: LH and FSH return to normal within 48 hours of the last dose [1]. That speed lets it be started partway through stimulation, which is shorter than the older long agonist protocol, where drugs such as leuprolide first trigger a hormone flare and then need a long down-regulation period before stimulation can begin [3].

Yes. The FDA approved ganirelix acetate injection in July 1999 [4]. Its label covers one use: inhibiting premature LH surges in women undergoing controlled ovarian hyperstimulation [1]. The label states that it should be prescribed by physicians experienced in infertility treatment [1].

blocks.text: Ganirelix is prescribed during IVF and related procedures, alongside FSH injections that grow the follicles. In the approval trials, it was started on day 6 of FSH and continued until follicles were large enough for the final trigger injection [1]. A dose-finding study in 332 patients found the highest pregnancy and implantation rates at the 250 mcg dose, which became the marketed strength [1].

The trial authors concluded that ganirelix gave similar pregnancy rates with a shorter course and fewer injections [2]. A 2016 Cochrane review pooled 73 randomized trials with 12,212 participants comparing GnRH antagonists against long agonist protocols. It found no clear difference in live birth rates, while antagonists lowered the odds of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), a potentially serious overreaction of the ovaries, by roughly 40% [3].

The same review found no difference in miscarriage rates. Cycles run with an antagonist were less often cancelled because of a high OHSS risk, but more often cancelled because the ovaries responded poorly [3]. Those trade-offs are part of why clinics choose between protocols case by case rather than using one for everyone.

In the controlled trials, side effects were recorded from the first injection until pregnancy was confirmed, so they reflect the whole IVF cycle and not ganirelix alone. Events seen in at least 1% of the 794 treated women included [1]:

items: Fetal loss (3.7%), which reflects early pregnancy outcomes in an IVF population [1]

blocks.text: Rare allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, swelling, and hives, have been reported after approval, sometimes with the first dose [1]. Ganirelix is contraindicated in known or suspected pregnancy and in people allergic to it or to other GnRH drugs [1]. A study of more than 1,000 newborns found birth defect rates similar to those after cycles using a GnRH agonist [1].
